headline: US survey finds chronic cough in IPF and other ILD affects daily life, sleep and emotional well-being
dek: A survey of 197 US adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or non-IPF interstitial lung disease found widespread physical, emotional and social effects of chronic cough, with limited relief from treatment.
body:
A cross-sectional survey of patients with interstitial lung disease (ILD) and chronic cough has reported substantial effects on daily activities, sleep, mood and relationships. The findings, from a team led by Jeffrey Swigris, Tejaswini Kulkarni and Charlene Watterston, are published in Chest.

The online survey was distributed to adults from June to July 2025 through the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation's US Community Registry. Participants needed a self-reported diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) or non-IPF ILD, and chronic cough, defined as lasting at least eight weeks. Questions covered demographics, disease history, cough characteristics, daily life impact, social and emotional and long-term impact, and healthcare experience.

In total, 197 participants completed the survey. Of these, 75.63% reported a diagnosis of IPF, 21.32% reported non-IPF ILD, and 3.05% were awaiting further ILD diagnosis. In the preceding week, 76.15% reported cough-related interference with daily activities and 79.69% reported sleep disruption.

Emotional burden was frequently reported: 95.94% had cough-induced worry, 75.13% reported depression, sadness or low mood, and 67.01% said they avoided social situations because of cough. Some 60.91% said chronic cough affected their platonic relationships, and 55.33% reported an impact on their ability or desire to maintain physical or intimate relationships.

Participants reported using an average of 2.7 therapeutic classes historically and 2.0 classes currently to treat cough, with many reporting limited or no relief. The authors concluded that, among respondents, the burden of chronic cough is physical, psychological and psychosocial, and that reports of limited relief suggest an unmet need in managing chronic cough in this population.

The abstract notes that the survey relied on self-reported diagnoses.
key_quote: chronic cough burden manifests physically, psychologically, and psychosocially

issues: The article says the findings are "from a team led by Jeffrey Swigris, Tejaswini Kulkarni and Charlene Watterston". The source only lists them as authors, followed by "et al.", and says nothing about who led the team. The "led by" role is unsupported, and it gives the three named authors a status the source does not.

Minor: "The abstract notes that the survey relied on self-reported diagnoses" frames an eligibility criterion as a limitation the abstract acknowledges. The abstract states only that eligibility required a self-reported diagnosis.

headline: Early-life LPG cooking did not improve lung function in Peruvian pre-schoolers versus biomass, follow-up finds
dek: A follow-up of a randomised trial in Peru found no overall difference in oscillometric lung function between children whose households used LPG and those using solid fuel.
body:
Early-life use of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for cooking did not improve lung function in pre-school children compared with exposure to biomass smoke, according to a study published in Pediatric Pulmonology.

The researchers, led by Laura Nicolaou, William Checkley and Jennifer Rha and colleagues, performed respiratory oscillometry in 3-5-year-olds whose mothers had taken part in a randomised trial of LPG versus usual solid fuel use during pregnancy and infancy. They tested 101 children, with a mean age of 4.4 years; 51.5% were male and 50.5% were in the intervention group.

Mean z-scores for resistance at 7 Hertz (R7), reactance at 7 Hertz (X7), resonance frequency (fres) and area above the reactance curve (AX7) were similar between the intervention and control groups. For AX7, the scores were 1.2 and 1.3 respectively. Intention-to-treat analysis showed no differences between arms in pre-bronchodilator lung function or bronchodilator response. The one exception was a larger post-bronchodilator decrease in mean fres z-score in the intervention arm (-0.36, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02).

In exposure-response analyses, postnatal carbon monoxide (CO) exposure was associated with higher AX7 z-scores, indicating worse reactance (0.041 per 1 ppm CO increase, 95% CI 0.003 to 0.078). No associations were found for PM2.5 exposure.

The authors described the CO finding as exploratory and said it warrants confirmation in larger cohorts. They noted that billions of people worldwide are exposed to household air pollution from solid fuel use.
key_quote: Early-life LPG use did not improve oscillometric lung function compared with those exposed to biomass smoke.

issues: The article says the researchers were "led by Laura Nicolaou, William Checkley and Jennifer Rha". The source only lists them as authors ("et al.") and says nothing about who led the study. Calling all three leaders is an unsupported claim about their roles.

source.title: Effects of Cooking With Liquefied Petroleum Gas or Biomass on Lung Function Among Pre-School Aged Children in Peru: A Prospective Follow-Up of a Randomized Trial.
source.author_name: Laura Nicolaou, William Checkley, Jennifer Rha et al.

headline: Cochrane review: pulmonary rehabilitation after COPD exacerbation likely reduces readmissions and improves quality of life
dek: An updated Cochrane review of 40 randomised trials found moderate-certainty evidence of fewer hospital readmissions and high-certainty evidence of better quality of life and exercise capacity.
body:
Pulmonary rehabilitation after an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) likely reduces hospital readmissions and produces large gains in quality of life and exercise capacity, according to an updated Cochrane review published in The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. The review was led by Manuel Weber, Elena Gimeno-Santos, Marieke Wuyts and colleagues.

The update added 20 studies to reach a total of 40 randomised controlled trials with 2,825 participants. All compared pulmonary rehabilitation of any duration, including at least exercise training, with usual care without rehabilitation. Searches were current to 2 June 2026. The programmes varied widely in exercise type, intensity and supervision, in patient education, and in how they were organised.

For hospital readmissions, 13 studies (1,229 participants) gave moderate-certainty evidence of a likely reduction (pooled odds ratio 0.52, 95% confidence interval 0.32 to 0.84). For all-cause mortality, low-certainty evidence suggested rehabilitation may reduce deaths slightly (pooled OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.43), based on 11 trials in the pooled estimate.

High-certainty evidence showed a large improvement in health-related quality of life. On the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score, the mean difference was -9.05 points (95% CI -12.60 to -5.50), beyond the minimal important difference of four points. Six-minute walk distance improved by a mean of 57.79 m (95% CI 41.68 to 73.91). Heterogeneity was substantial for both outcomes.

The authors noted that some recent studies found no benefit on readmissions and mortality. They suggested this may be explained partly by how extensive the programmes were and by study quality. Tests showed funnel plot asymmetry for readmissions and mortality, which the authors said was more consistent with small-study effects than with missing negative studies. The lack of participant blinding raised concerns for subjectively reported outcomes such as quality of life.

The authors wrote that further trials comparing rehabilitation with no rehabilitation seem questionable scientifically and ethically. They said future research should examine how programmes can be designed and implemented to be feasible, cost-effective and accessible, and how their organisation within healthcare systems affects readmissions and mortality. The review had no dedicated funding.
key_quote: Moderate-certainty evidence indicates that pulmonary rehabilitation likely reduces hospital readmissions, while evidence for mortality is of low certainty.

headline: CHMP recommends sintilimab plus chemotherapy for first-line nonsquamous NSCLC
dek: The EMA committee backed the PD-1 inhibitor with pemetrexed and platinum-based chemotherapy; a European Commission decision is expected in the coming months.
body:
The Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) of the European Medicines Agency has issued a positive opinion recommending marketing authorisation of sintilimab (Zybrivo), a PD-1 inhibitor, in combination with pemetrexed and platinum-based chemotherapy. The proposed indication is first-line treatment of adult patients with nonsquamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including locally advanced disease that cannot be managed with curative-intent surgery or chemoradiation, and metastatic disease. The European Commission is expected to issue a final decision in the coming months, according to OnLive's report.

The recommendation was based on the randomised, double-blind phase 3 ORIENT-11 trial (NCT03607539), which enrolled 397 adults with locally advanced, metastatic or recurrent nonsquamous NSCLC with no detectable EGFR or ALK aberrations, irrespective of PD-L1 expression. Patients were randomised 2:1 to sintilimab or placebo, each with pemetrexed and platinum-based chemotherapy. The primary end point was progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by a blinded independent radiological review committee.

Sintilimab plus chemotherapy was associated with a 52% lower risk of disease progression or death. Median PFS was 8.9 months versus 5.0 months. Median overall survival (OS) was 24.2 months versus 16.8 months (HR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.50-0.85), and estimated 2-year OS rates were 50% versus 32%. After adjustment for crossover, the OS hazard ratio was 0.52 (95% CI, 0.38-0.69). The safety profile was in line with those of PD-1 inhibitors and the chemotherapy agents used, with no new safety signals.

Dr Hui Zhou, chief R&D officer of Oncology at Innovent, said in a news release that the opinion "marks an important regulatory milestone in our international development".

In the United States, the FDA issued a complete response letter on 24 March 2022 for the sintilimab application, after a 10 February 2022 meeting of its Oncologic Drugs Advisory Committee. The committee voted 14 to 1 that a new trial representative of the US population was needed, noting that the ORIENT-11 population was younger, predominantly male and included more smokers than typical US patients.
key_quote: The positive CHMP opinion for [sintilimab] marks an important regulatory milestone in our international development and brings us a step closer to serving patients in Europe

The body attributes the report to "OnLive's report". The source is from OncLive, so the outlet name is wrong and is not supported by the source.

The article is thin. It restates the headline in three different ways: the coalition's call, the AIR health workforce pillar, and 'the message ... is that healthcare workers should be central'. It also pads with 'The ERS post links to further information'. A reader learns nothing beyond the headline, such as who the other coalition members are or what the pillar would involve.
The 'air-pollution' tag is not supported by the source, which does not mention air pollution.

headline: ERS issues first guideline on managing idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with concomitant lung cancer
dek: A European Respiratory Society Task Force made 11 conditional recommendations, weighing oncological benefit against treatment toxicity in patients with both conditions.
body:
A European Respiratory Society (ERS) task force has produced a clinical practice guideline for patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and lung cancer, published in The European Respiratory Journal. The authors say managing the two conditions together is a major clinical challenge because of increased incidence and a negative effect on quality of life and mortality, and that evidence-based recommendations have been lacking.

The multidisciplinary Task Force included experts and patient representatives. It produced 11 conditional recommendations across seven PICO questions and two narrative questions; no recommendation was issued for one PICO question. Systematic reviews were carried out for each question, evidence certainty was assessed using GRADE, and recommendations were formulated using the Evidence-to-Decision framework.

For early-stage lung cancer, the Task Force suggests surgical resection in medically fit patients. It says postoperative risk requires systematic preoperative evaluation, discussion of perioperative antifibrotic therapy and protective perioperative strategies. For stereotactic radiotherapy, it issued a conditional recommendation for either the intervention or the comparison, balancing potential oncological benefit against radiation pneumonitis.

In locally advanced disease, the Task Force suggests not giving concurrent radio-chemotherapy because of very high acute exacerbation rates. For advanced lung cancer, chemotherapy is suggested in medically fit patients, where survival benefits outweigh increased toxicity risks. For stage IV disease, evidence for immunotherapy was limited, so a conditional recommendation for either the intervention or the comparison was issued. Evidence on targeted therapy was insufficient to support a recommendation.

The authors conclude that, given the poor prognosis of both conditions and the risks of treatment, management requires multidisciplinary assessment of competing risks and patient preferences in experienced interstitial lung disease and oncology centres.
key_quote: For advanced lung cancer, chemotherapy is suggested in medically fit patients, where survival benefits outweigh increased toxicity risks.

issues: The headline calls this the "first guideline" on IPF with concomitant lung cancer. The source never says it is the first. It says only that evidence-based recommendations are lacking, so "first" is unsupported and overstates the source.

source.title: ERS clinical practice guidelines for the management of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and lung cancer.

headline: AIHW data show lung cancer survival in Australia has improved but inequities persist
dek: Lung Foundation Australia said new Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data show lung cancer remains the country's leading cause of cancer death.
body:
Lung Foundation Australia has highlighted new data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) on the impact of lung cancer in Australia. The organisation shared the findings on LinkedIn during Lung Cancer Awareness Month, observed in November.

According to the foundation's summary of the data, survival rates have improved. However, lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death in Australia.

The foundation said significant inequities persist for First Nations peoples, people living in disadvantaged areas, and people in regional and remote communities.

The post directs readers to a series of key findings and an online overview of the AIHW data. Lung Foundation Australia also said that specialist lung cancer nurses are available through its Lung Health Helpline and website chat function, with translation offered in several languages.
key_quote: significant inequities persist for First Nations peoples, people living in disadvantaged areas, and regional and remote communities

issues: The article is thin. The source post gives no figures, survival rates, dates or findings from the AIHW data, and the article adds nothing beyond the headline. Its body restates the headline and dek, then says the post 'directs readers to a series of key findings and an online overview', which amounts to saying the source gives no details. The helpline and nurse paragraph is promotional filler, not news. A reader learns almost nothing beyond the headline.

The headline says 'AIHW data show...', but the source is only a Lung Foundation Australia social post summarising the data. The article never saw the AIHW data itself, so the headline is presented more firmly than the source supports, though the body does attribute the claim to the foundation's summary.

headline: Allergy may begin with barrier-cell energy failure rather than the immune system, Griffith-led study proposes
dek: A Griffith University-led analysis of multi-omic data suggests mitochondrial dysfunction in epithelial barrier cells may precede allergic disease, though the authors describe it as a hypothesis to be tested.
body:
Allergies may originate in a power failure inside the cells that line the body's barriers, rather than in the immune system, according to a study led by Griffith University. The cells in question line the skin, gut, nose, lungs and oesophagus.

The team analysed what study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist at Griffith's School of Medicine and Dentistry, described as the largest multi-omic collection of allergy data it was aware of. It covered 116 case-control cohorts, 3,776 patients and 2,164 cohorts. "For 60 years, we've taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around," he said.

The researchers propose that mitochondria in epithelial cells fail to meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment, so the barrier cell "raises the alarm too easily" and the immune events recognised as allergy follow. The evidence was strongest in eosinophilic oesophagitis, where the programme cells use to clear damaged mitochondria was reduced in all 13 independent patient cohorts. In eczema, changes to the skin's barrier and antioxidant defences were found even in non-inflamed skin.

The signal was not present in every condition. It was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps, and only partly present in hay fever. The paper also argued that many triggers, including processed diets, pollution, microplastics, detergents, loss of dietary fibre and early antibiotics, act on one shared target: the energy capacity of the barrier cell.

Co-author Associate Professor Nic West, a molecular immunologist at Griffith's School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences, said current drugs act downstream, so disease often returns when treatment stops. Professor Smith said the team was clear this was a hypothesis, not a settled mechanism, and that the next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before allergy develops.

The paper, "The origins of allergy: An outside-in, bioenergetic hypothesis", is published in Allergy. Co-authors were from Mount Sinai, Leuven, Cork, Southampton, Zurich, Miami, Singapore and Aberdeen.
key_quote: This is not a cure but is something we have never had before – a logical starting point.

headline: Negative low-dose CT result linked to long-term lung cancer risks comparable with low-risk population
dek: Original research in CHEST indicates that people with negative low-dose CT screening results had long-term outcomes similar to the low-risk population, according to the journal's announcement.
body:
Individuals with negative low-dose CT screening results generally had long-term risks of lung cancer incidence, lung cancer mortality and all-cause mortality comparable with those of the low-risk population, according to original research published in the November issue of the journal CHEST.

The American College of Chest Physicians (CHEST) highlighted the findings in a post on X on 20 November 2026. The post said the results support risk-stratified follow-up rather than uniform annual rescreening.

The three outcomes compared were lung cancer incidence, lung cancer mortality and death from any cause. According to the post, the similarity to the low-risk population applied to people with negative screening results generally, rather than in every case.

The full paper is available in the November issue of CHEST.
key_quote: supporting risk-stratified follow-up rather than uniform annual rescreening

issues: The article is thin. The source is a single short promotional post, and the article only restates its headline claim. It gives no study design, population, follow-up length, numbers, authors or paper title, so a reader learns nothing beyond the headline.

Several sentences pad rather than inform. These are the sentence listing the three outcomes already named in the lede, the line 'The full paper is available in the November issue of CHEST', and the sentence about the post's own attribution.

The sentence 'applied to people with negative screening results generally, rather than in every case' goes beyond the source. The post says only 'generally', and the article builds a separate point on that one word.
The dek says 'according to the journal's announcement', but the post came from the American College of Chest Physicians' account, not the journal's. This is a minor attribution blur.

headline: Cash incentives nearly double quit rates among underserved adults in lung screening trial
dek: A JAMA randomised trial of more than 3,200 people referred for lung cancer screening found payments of up to $600 improved smoking cessation compared with usual care.
body:
Offering financial incentives of up to $600 nearly doubled smoking cessation rates among medically underserved adults undergoing lung cancer screening, according to a randomised clinical trial published in JAMA. Penn Medicine Cancer highlighted the findings on X.

The study was led by researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania and collaborators nationwide. It enrolled more than 3,200 patients who were referred for low-dose CT lung cancer screening and still smoked, across Penn Medicine, Geisinger, Henry Ford Health and Kaiser Permanente Southern California. Participants were predominantly from groups that often face barriers to high-quality care, including people with lower incomes, those in rural communities, and Black and Hispanic adults.

The researchers tested four approaches: standard ask-advise-refer care; standard care plus free cessation medication; standard care plus free medication and financial incentives; and the same package plus FutureMe, a text-based behavioural tool that prompted participants to imagine their smoke-free future selves. Abstinence at six months was confirmed by blood or urine tests. Incentives produced higher quit rates than usual care and free medication alone. Payments were contingent on a verifying sample: $100 at two weeks, $200 at three months and $300 at six months.

"These participants had smoked for decades and likely made multiple unsuccessful quit attempts in the past," said senior author Scott D. Halpern, MD, PhD, director of the Palliative and Advanced Illness Research Center at Penn. He said adding incentives increased quit rates in a population that can be especially hard to reach with traditional approaches.

Joanna L. Hart, MD, the study's lead author and an assistant professor in Pulmonary, Allergy and Critical Care, said new approaches that help people stop smoking can have a large impact on health and quality of life. The study is believed to be the largest trial of financial incentives for smoking cessation among patients referred for lung cancer screening. The investigators are now examining how to implement incentive-based programmes more widely and studying public perceptions of paying people to quit. The work was funded by a PCORI award.
key_quote: These participants had smoked for decades and likely made multiple unsuccessful quit attempts in the past.

headline: Four abstracts at ACAAI 2026 examine gaps in asthma education, biologic access and steroid use
dek: Allergy & Asthma Network says it led and contributed to four abstracts presented at the ACAAI annual meeting in Phoenix, covering education, biologics, systemic corticosteroids and uncontrolled asthma.
body:
Allergy & Asthma Network said it led and contributed to four research abstracts presented at the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology (ACAAI) 2026 Annual Scientific Meeting, held 12–16 November at the Phoenix Convention Center in Arizona. The findings were presented as conference abstracts rather than in a journal.

One abstract, "Beyond Pharmacotherapy: Providing Comprehensive Asthma Education Is Essential For Achieving Optimal Asthma Control", was authored by Leandra Tonweber, Mitu Patel and De De Gardner. According to the network, it examined why education is an essential part of asthma management and argued that comprehensive education should accompany prescribed treatment. A second, by Patel and Gardner, is titled "Barriers to Biologic Medication Adoption for Patients with Uncontrolled and Severe Asthma". It looked at why some patients may face challenges accessing or starting biologic medicines.

Gardner also contributed to a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials, "Maintenance Systemic Corticosteroids for the Management of Asthma". It examined the benefits and risks of long-term systemic corticosteroid use. The network said patient partners Amanda Flowers, Hilarry Orr and Angel Melendez were coauthors.

The fourth abstract is titled "Uncontrolled Symptomatic Asthma Remains Poorly Recognized and Undertreated: Evidence from a Global Patient Survey". The network said it was produced in collaboration with Sanofi and involved Patel.

The network said the studies together underline the importance of understanding patients' experiences and improving access to care.
key_quote: Medication is important for controlling asthma, but patients also need reliable information and practical tools to manage their condition.

issues: The article is thin. It lists four abstract titles, authors and a one-line topic for each, but reports no findings, data or conclusions. A reader learns little beyond the headline and the titles.

"The findings were presented as conference abstracts rather than in a journal" is not supported. The source says the abstracts were presented at ACAAI but does not say whether they were published in a journal. The article also calls them "findings" when the source reports none.
The key quote is a press-release sentence presented as a standalone quote with no attribution. It could be read as coming from a named person, when it is the organisation's own text.

source.title: Allergy & Asthma Network highlights research on gaps in asthma care at ACAAI 2026

extra.scout_summary: The network led or contributed to four abstracts at the ACAAI 2026 meeting (12–16 November, Phoenix). The studies address the role of asthma education beyond medication, barriers to biologic uptake in severe uncontrolled asthma, risks of long-term steroid use, and under-recognition of uncontrolled asthma.
